projects.title: Airflow ETL Pipeline
projects.tools: Apache Airflow, Python, PostgreSQL, Docker, AWS instance

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Built a production ETL platform on Apache Airflow 2.8.1 (Docker Compose) that consolidates SQL Server and 10 third-party APIs into a single SQL Server warehouse, using a Bronze → Silver → Gold medallion architecture to move raw data through cleansing and business-ready transformation layers.

Platform runs 11 orchestrated DAGs on a weekly schedule, each following the same standardized extract → cleanse → transform pattern, feeding  gold-layer business tables used for downstream reporting.

blocks.heading: ROLE
blocks.body:
Designed the medallion architecture and DAG pattern (parallel bronze/silver extraction fanning into a single gold transform) that all 11 pipelines are built on.
Built the core SQL Server pipeline first — extracting 4 source tables and modeling them into 4 gold business tables (daily sales by SKU/channel, monthly channel performance, product catalog, unified daily product performance).

Wrote a shared Python data access layer (db_connection.py) handling chunked reads/writes, bulk-load performance tuning, automatic schema drift handling, and JSON serialization — reused across every pipeline instead of rebuilding logic per source.

Developed 10 API extractor modules (Amazon Ads, Amazon Vendor Central, Shopify, Zendesk, Klaviyo, Wayfair, BazaarVoice, Salsify, MySamm, Sage 300/HIP) on a shared base class handling auth, retries, and pagination. Implemented incremental/watermark-based loading (using python) so pipelines pull only new or changed records, with custom watermark logic where a source's default update behavior didn't fit.
Containerized the stack (custom Dockerfile with ODBC Driver 18) and wrote environment-driven connection bootstrap scripts for repeatable setup.
Documented the system end to end — an operator's manual for running/troubleshooting the stack and a full technical reference covering every DAG, script, and config variable

blocks.heading: Challenges & learnings
blocks.body:
SQL Server column/row limits on wide data: Salsify's product exports exceeded SQL Server's 1024-column and ~8060-byte row caps — solved by packing overflow fields into a JSON column instead of failing the load.

Data type incompatibility: pandas didn't support SQL Server's datetimeoffset type (ODBC type -155), breaking reads — resolved by casting to datetime2 at the query level.
Inconsistent incremental semantics across APIs: each platform tracked "updated" records differently (some by date, some by timestamp, some not reliably at all), requiring per-source watermark logic rather than one generic solution. 

API data bifurcation: The Sage 300/HIP integration had containerized/nested JSON information fields this required SQL command which required Column identification and separation into their own distinct columns. 

Schema drift from external APIs: incoming API fields changed shape or type over time (e.g., a column that was numeric started receiving text) — handled with automatic column widening and type migration in the write layer rather than manual fixes each time.

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body: Led the rebuild of the company's sales and inventory reporting dashboard, which the sales, merchandising, and operations teams rely on to track weekly and monthly performance. The project involved cleaning up and validating the numbers behind the dashboard, moving the underlying data off a single laptop and onto shared, always-on company infrastructure, and tracking down the source of several long-standing data gaps that had never been fully explained.

blocks.heading: ROLE AND TASKS
blocks.body:
• End-to-end rebuild of the reporting dashboard, working directly from the business's reporting requirements to make sure every chart and table was pulling from the right, verified data.

• Migrated the company's core sales, inventory, and customer records off a single employee workspace and onto a shared company server, so the data would be reliably available to everyone rather than depending on one machine. Copied over 400,000 records across 14 datasets and independently verified every single one matched exactly before considering the
move complete.

• Found and fixed several calculation errors that had been quietly producing misleading numbers on the original dashboard (averaging and summations) and, including a percentage total that was inflating to over 600,000% and a date label that was off by a day.

• Designed and stood up a new automated daily inventory tracking process, replacing manual, one-off checks with a system that captures a full snapshot of stock levels every day.

• Rebuilt and validated 25 of the dashboard's report pages, confirming each one showed sensible, accurate figures before signing off.

• Investigated a long-standing data gap affecting thousands of products missing key catalog information, systematically checking every plausible data source before documenting a clear, evidence-backed conclusion for the business.

• Diagnosed recurring “why isn't my data showing up” complaints from report users, tracing them back to how the dashboard's date filters worked rather than a data problem — saving time on future troubleshooting.

blocks.heading: Challenges & learnings
blocks.body:
• The data migration (Staging to Live)  wasn't as simple as copying files over — a technical limitation in the original migration approach meant switching tools partway through as Db-to-Db transfer was not possible because of  ID columns had auto incrementing on and original referenced tables would break, therefore had to utilize Import/export wizard, and I learned to double-check that each setting had actually been applied rather than assuming the tool saved it.

• Several data tables looked, based on their names, like they would hold the answer to a missing-data question — but turned out to hold something completely (Like category table instead of category info it had accounting/ledger info) different once actually opened. This reinforced a habit I carried through the whole project: always confirm what a table actually contains before relying on it, rather than trusting how it's labeled.

• Tracking down “missing” data taught me to compare the original source and the report side by side before assuming something was broken — more than once, what looked like a data problem turned out to be a display or filtering quirk.

•  Investigations on collection information required ruling out every technical explanation before concluding that the real answer had to come from the business rather than the data itself (Collection was stored in a different source "Salsify" as compared to sales data "Sage"). That thoroughness turned out to be just as valuable as fixing a bug — it gave stakeholders confidence that nothing had been missed.

projects.title: Chronic AI App
projects.tools: Python, Azure Blob container, Azure Synapse

blocks.heading: OVERVIEW
blocks.body:
The Chronic AI is a healthcare project that combines data science, machine learning, and a conversational AI assistant to support patients managing diabetes and cardiovascular disease. 

The system draws on real patient health information — demographics, diet, lifestyle habits, mental health, medical history, and medication — to power an AI chat assistant that gives patients personalized, round-the-clock coaching, while giving clinicians a clear,
transparent view into how each recommendation was reached.

blocks.heading: ROLE
blocks.body:
• Built the first stage of the project's data pipeline: sourcing raw patient and health data from multiple separate origins and bringing it all into one central storage location (Azure Blob) so it could be cleaned and used downstream.

• Pulled together seven distinct categories of patient data — demographics, dietary habits, lifestyle indicators, mental health, medical reports, medication records, and physical activity — from their original raw files. Publicly listed.

• Brought in outside reference data (published Australian diabetes research and national statistics) to ground the project's health-risk models in real-world context, alongside the patient-level data.

• Loaded all of this raw data into a cloud data lake container and a database, forming the foundation layer that every later step — cleaning, modeling, and the AI assistant itself — was built on top of.

blocks.heading: Challenges & learnings
blocks.body:
• The data sources each came from a different origin and didn't line up neatly with one another — patient ID formats, date formats, and record structures all differed and had to be reconciled before the data was usable.

• Some sources contained duplicate records and inconsistent text formatting (stray spaces, inconsistent capitalization), which needed to be standardized so nothing was double-counted or mismatched later.

• Making sure a given patient's records actually lined up correctly across all seven datasets took extra care — a mismatch at this stage could silently disconnect someone's diet data from their medical history further down the pipeline.

• A number of the source files had missing or incomplete entries, requiring judgment calls on how to handle the gaps without skewing the health-risk models built later.

sections.heading: About
sections.body: Data Engineer specializing in ETL pipelines and Power BI reporting, with hands-on experience building production data platforms end-to-end. Designed a containerized Apache Airflow platform using a Bronze/Silver/Gold Medallion architecture to integrate 10+ REST/GraphQL APIs into a unified SQL Server warehouse, and delivered a ERP System-to-Power BI reporting pipeline with custom dimensional modelling and DAX measures — from source-system integration through to dashboard delivery and stakeholder-facing data quality troubleshooting.
